I have a point to make about cross-over threads. They are generally a bad idea. They become extremely muddled when trying to adhere to a Watsonian framework. Trying to compare someone from the 40k universe to a Dragon Ball Z character quickly dissolves into nonsense because both have a very specific power hierarchy that doesn't really relate to reality.

In these instances it is more productive, and interesting, to compare how fictional content functions. Avoiding threads that ask "could x hero defeat y hero" might be useful in promoting good content.

With crossover threads, it really depends on the universes you're using and the question being asked. 40k vs DBZ is just generally a bad matchup because the respective universes are nothing alike. A Star Wars/Star Trek thread, however, would work out very well as the universes and technologies are very similar (though orders of magnitude apart). Crossover threads can also be used to, despite the inherent issue with meshing the two universes, foster an interesting discussion on something from one or both universes. For example, this thread would force the answerer to delve into the specifics of how the killing curse works as well as the true properties of Venom's control. There is definitely room for error, but given that we've only had one crossover thread so far and it got barely any attention since it was at the very start of the sub, I'm not too worried.

Avoiding threads that ask "could x hero defeat y hero" might be useful in promoting good content.

How long would a normal session last?

I'm not trying to be difficult when I say "it depends". While technically it can be as short as an hour or three, I find anything less than 4 hours to be too short. Depending on how quick your group gets into the proper mindset and what you're doing in the game you could accomplish a significant portion of the DM's current arc, or you could get halfway through a single battle.

As a frame of reference for you, my normal sessions of the last ~5 years I played (had to stop a little over a year ago due to not having as much free time) were about 12 hours every Sunday. In the other 10 some odd years I've played sessions averaged around 8 hours every handful of weeks.

If you're strapped for time, and also presuming you're the DM, I recommend you play it by ear the first few sessions to see how everyone does. You'll run into things such as some players not being able to pay attention (despite the fact that they aren't at work or school :/), the inability to do math (the stoners I've played with never had this issue, though), or my personal favorite, the player whose character never shuts up. We once spent over an hour on a 5 minute conversation. At any rate, once you get an idea of how your players will act, you'll be able to gauge how much story you can get through in your allotted time. If you don't have a hard limit on your time (FLGS closing for the night, for example), then just play until people start getting tired of playing.

Oh, and loosely related to session time are your dice. The DM should have at least 2 - 4 sets of dice, while the players should have at least 1 set each. Nothing like having to make a dozen rolls 1 die at a time. Ideally the players should look at what their characters are going to be able to do at higher levels and buy dice accordingly. Fighter-types typically don't have to worry about having a dozen d6s, but your local Wizard that throws around a few Fireballs and Chain Lightnings every battle better stock up so they don't spend 2 minutes figuring out how much damage they did after every spell.

You can roughly divide gameplay into 3 categories: social, environment, and battle.

Social would be the players interacting with NPCs. This could be anything from ordering food at a tavern to trying to get in bed with royalty. Literally. These interactions can be a means to an end, such as gaining access to an area without having to worry about the local law being on your case. It can also be the end itself, such as trying to negotiate peace between two ruling countries. Of course, if your players are malicious they can incite a war. Or just kill the royalty and take over themselves. I'll cover battle more later.

Environment and battle can go hand in hand, but not necessarily. This would be like your typical dungeon crawl. Think Indiana Jones and all the various places he raided. Every cave typically won't be lined with spear traps, spike pits, and rolling boulders, but the bigger dungeons that have treasure in them typically have something like that at least. Since magic (typically) exists in the world your average spear trap can be shooting lightning bolts instead, the spike pit instead is a one way ticket to the elemental plane of fire, and that rolling boulder is really a cranky beholder that's been magically locked up for too long. On top of that, they're also typically home to creatures that don't take kindly to robbers, which leads to battle.

Being a tabletop instead of a PC/video game means that battle can happen whenever a player starts it, so be prepared. This will likely be the most time consuming portion of gameplay until everyone knows what they want to do on their turn. As everyone gets higher in level, more options open up. Still, once everyone gets some playtime under their belts they'll be able to pretty quickly figure out what they want to do when their turn rolls around.

That's not to say that these are the only things you can do in the game. You could have tournaments of skill, spend time just crafting, chill in an inn planning your next move, build a castle, or any number of other things. The big three above, though, are typically the meat and potatoes for gamers, with anything extra a bonus.

That depends on a lot of things, actually. Are you and your group looking to do some roleplaying or rollplaying? Do you have a lot of time to dedicate to each session, or is it going to be in short sittings? I know you mentioned below that nobody is well versed in tabletop gaming, but there are a handful of PC games (Neverwinter Nights primarily) that play fairly close to D&D's rules. Have any of you played those? Finally, how married are you to playing D&D, and not one of its alternatives like Fantasy Craft or Pathfinder.

I wholly recommend 5th edition. Bounded Accuracy, inter-class balance (no tier nonsense here), good differentiation between classes, and streamlined/simplified mechanics such as (dis)Advantage. The Backgrounds mechanic also helps players get into roleplaying if they are not quite sure where to start. Also, the Magic Item Mart™ is no longer present.

If I had to pick a runner-up, I would hesitantly recommend 4E if you're coming from video games. Balance is also there (for the most part), but classes are more homogenous. It's also more of a combat sim, so prepare for long battles.

5e is the easiest to jump into with new players in my opinion, particularly if everyone including the DM is new. 5e reads clearly, the only confusions I ever had with it were based on me being rooted in older versions and adapting to the differences. There's a tremendous amount of help on the internet right now for it, and if you don't want to homebrew the campaign there are the pre-made well designed campaigns made by WotC in Tyranny of Dragons and the new one that just came out, Elemental Evil.

It's the most well rounded version in my opinion, which is huge for new players because it will allow your group to play and get a feel for what elements of the game you enjoy the most, and it will have you covered if you want to delve into them. You might find you want the sessions to be combat heavy, rolling lots of dice and slicing lots of bad guys up. 5e has you covered, it's a fun combat system that's easy to understand. If you decide your group is really getting into playing their character and doing some real role playing and influencing the world outside of combat, it's got you covered there too, and in a fairly cohesive way. Some would argue that 3.5 is much better for roleplaying and 4e is better for combat, but both of them are lacking in the alternatives. 5e is the most balanced, the most zen of the releases.

(Obviously just my opinion. Don't get all only-my-version-is-good-fan-boy on me, please. <3)
